slides.title: What government does
slides.notes: Name what a government does and give one rule that affects daily life. Notes: use the school as a model; learners list who makes the rules, who enforces them and who can ask for a change.

slides.title: Rights, duties and voting
slides.slide: L2 Awareness · Rights, duties and voting
slides.notes: Explain a right, a duty and why people vote. Notes: learners hold a class vote on one real choice and note who did not vote and why; discuss whether a result is fair if only half take part.

slides.title: Constitutions and electoral systems
slides.slide: L3 Foundation · Constitutions and electoral systems
slides.notes: Describe separation of powers and compare plurality and proportional voting. Notes: three parties win 40, 35 and 25 per cent; proportional voting in 100 seats gives 40, 35 and 25, whereas a seat can be won with 40 per cent under plurality.

slides.title: Comparing political systems
slides.notes: Compare parliamentary and presidential systems and measure disproportionality. Notes: votes of 45, 35 and 20 per cent with seats of 55, 30 and 15 give gaps of 10, 5 and 5; half the sum is 10 points; learners say which system helps small parties.

slides.title: Power, ideology and coalitions
slides.slide: L5 Specialist · Power, ideology and coalitions
slides.notes: Analyse sovereignty, ideology and a coalition problem in a 100-seat house. Notes: parties hold 48, 30 and 22 seats and need 51; every pair has a majority, so the 30 and 22 seat parties could together exclude the largest.

slides.title: Institutions and party systems
slides.slide: L6 Advanced · Institutions and party systems
slides.notes: Evaluate how institutions shape the number of parties and policy stability. Notes: vote shares 0.5, 0.3 and 0.2 give an effective number of parties of about 2.63; learners compare it with a two-party case and discuss veto players.

slides.title: Causal inference in comparative politics
slides.slide: L7 Super expert · Causal inference in comparative politics
slides.notes: Design a comparative study and defend an estimate of a policy effect. Notes: treated turnout moves from 50 to 58 and control from 52 to 55, so the difference in differences is 5 points; test the parallel-trends assumption and list threats.
